\documentclass{article}
\title{A Simulator for Dendrite Growth in Solid-State Batteries}
\author{W. Kaczmarek}
\date{May 2026}
\begin{document}
\maketitle
\section{Introduction}
Solid-state batteries promise higher energy density and improved safety,
but lithium filaments still penetrate the solid electrolyte at practical currents.
We built a phase field simulator that resolves filament nucleation and growth
at the interface between the metal anode and a sulphide electrolyte.

\section{Cell Model}
The model couples electrostatics, stress, and interfacial kinetics.
A Butler-Volmer condition sets the deposition rate at the interface,
and mechanical stress feeds back on the local exchange current.
The electrolyte is treated as a linear elastic solid,
while the lithium electrode creeps on the time scale of deposition.

\section{Numerical Solver}
The governing equations are discretised on an adaptive grid.
An implicit time stepper handles the stiff kinetics,
and a geometric multigrid preconditioner solves the resulting linear systems.
Mesh refinement follows the filament tip
so that the high curvature region is always well resolved.

\section{Implementation}
The reference implementation is written in the C# programming language
and ships with a small scripting interface for parameter sweeps.
All results in this paper can be reproduced with the published input decks,
and the continuous integration farm reruns the benchmarks nightly.

\section{Validation}
The solver is validated against an analytical sharp interface solution
for a growing hemispherical filament.
Convergence is second order in space and first order in time,
in line with the design of the discretisation.
Computed onset currents match the validation experiments within their error bars.

\section{Results}
Simulations reproduce the experimentally observed onset of filament growth
and predict a strong dependence on stack pressure.
Holding the cell above the critical pressure suppresses nucleation entirely
in the parameter window we explored.
Lower temperatures shift the onset to higher currents,
consistent with the Arrhenius scaling of the exchange current.

\section{Performance}
A typical two dimensional run completes in under an hour on a desktop workstation.
Three dimensional runs are distributed across a small cluster
and scale well to a few hundred cores for the grid sizes used here.

\section{Outlook}
Future work will couple the model to tomography data from operando cells
and will explore electrolytes with graded mechanical properties.
\end{document}
